metaTitle: 6 Best Loppers for Tree and Shrub Trimming 2026
metaDescription: Six loppers compared on bypass vs anvil heads, cutting capacity, handle length and leverage mechanisms for pruning branches safely and easily.
introParagraphs: A lopper is the tool you pick up when a branch is too thick for hand pruners and not worth a saw. Long handles multiply your arm strength, and the cutting head decides what the tool is good at: bypass blades slice live green wood like scissors, while anvil heads press a blade onto a flat plate to crack through dry, dead limbs. Buying the wrong head for your yard is the most common mistake.

We evaluated six loppers that span the useful range: a Fiskars 32 inch PowerGear2 bypass with a 2 inch capacity, a Corona X Series Pro bypass rated to 2-1/4 inches, a TABOR TOOLS GG12A 30 inch compound anvil, a 36 inch Hickok with aluminum handles, a short 20 inch FELCO F211-50, and a Prunrt telescopic model with a sync drive mechanism. The comparison looks at head type, stated capacity, handle length and what each listing actually promises.

Capacity ratings assume fresh green wood, and dry hardwood is harder than the number suggests, so we point out where a stronger mechanism or a saw is the wiser answer. The tables below match each pick to your pruning job.

products.name: Fiskars 32 Inch PowerGear2 Bypass Lopper, 2 Inch Cut
products.description:
The Fiskars PowerGear2 pairs a 32 inch bypass head with a leverage mechanism the listing says multiplies cutting power over traditional designs. It is rated to cut branches up to 2 inches thick, and the fully hardened steel blade carries a low friction coating that the listing says reduces gumming from sap.

Bypass blades are the right choice for live wood, because they slice rather than crush and leave a cleaner wound on the plant. Two inches is at the top of what a homeowner lopper usually claims, so it handles most shrubs and fruit tree branches. Because the capacity assumes green wood, expect dry hardwood to need a saw or a stronger tool. At 32 inches it is long enough for good leverage without becoming unwieldy.

Ownership is easy: wipe the blade after sappy work, keep the pivot snug and sharpen the cutting edge when it starts to crush rather than slice. Compared with the 28 inch Fiskars class it adds length and a larger capacity, and compared with the Corona X Series Pro at 2-1/4 inches it gives up a little capacity. It is the most balanced lopper in this group for a typical yard.
products.bestFor: Most homeowners pruning shrubs and live branches up to 2 inches.
pros: Bypass blade for clean cuts on live wood

products.name: Corona X Series Pro Bypass Lopper, 2-1/4 Inch Cut
products.description:
Corona claims the largest capacity in this group at 2-1/4 inches, using a precision bypass blade with a scissor style action. The listing says the bypass design slices smoothly through live wood, reducing crushing and helping healthy cuts, and describes a heavy duty pro grade build for repeated use.

The extra quarter inch over a standard 2 inch lopper matters when you face the occasional thicker limb on a tree you maintain every year. The listing does not give a handle length or a leverage mechanism name in the text we evaluated, so check the product page for weight and length, since a bigger tool is heavier to swing. A heavy tool tires hands quickly on a long afternoon.

In use, it behaves like any quality bypass lopper: align the cut, squeeze steadily and avoid twisting the blade in the wood. Compared with the Fiskars PowerGear2 it offers more capacity but no stated leverage system, and compared with the TABOR anvil it is for live wood. It suits owners with mature trees.
products.bestFor: Owners of mature trees who face thicker live limbs each season.
pros: Slices rather than crushes live wood
cons: Length and weight need a page check

products.name: TABOR TOOLS GG12A 30 Inch Anvil Lopper, Compound Action
products.description:
TABOR TOOLS pairs an anvil head with a compound action mechanism that the listing says multiplies cutting power for dry, dead and woody branches. It is a 30 inch tool described as chopping through 2 inch branches, with a hardened carbon steel blade and a low friction non stick coating.

Anvil loppers crush against a flat surface, which is ideal for dead wood and a poor match for live green stems that can be squashed. Use this one for deadheading and clearing dry branches, and keep a bypass tool for living growth. The 30 inch length adds leverage, and rubberized grips help a secure hold. The listing states a capacity but does not say whether it is for dry or green wood, so treat 2 inches as a ceiling.

Ownership is simple: keep the blade sharp and clean, and avoid twisting while cutting. Compared with the Fiskars PowerGear2 it is for a different job, and compared with the 36 inch Hickok it is shorter and has steel handles. Choose it when your yard has more dead wood than green.
products.bestFor: Clearing dry, dead and woody branches with strong leverage.
cons: Anvil head can crush live stems
Capacity not tied to dry or green wood

products.name: Hickok Heavy Duty Loppers, 36 Inch Aluminum Handles
products.description:
Hickok stretches to 36 inches with aircraft grade aluminum handles that the listing says are strong yet light, reducing fatigue. The blade is forged, hardened and heat treated steel, and the listing promotes extended reach and cutting power for high branches.

The length is the key feature here, since longer handles give you more leverage and reach higher into a shrub or hedge. The tradeoff is control: a long lopper is harder to place precisely in dense growth. The listing does not state a cutting capacity or whether the head is bypass or anvil in the text we evaluated, so check the product page for both numbers before relying on it for thick limbs.

In ownership the aluminum helps, because a 36 inch steel lopper would be heavy by the end of an afternoon. Compared with the 30 inch Hickok it adds six inches of reach, and compared with the 20 inch FELCO it is a reach tool. It suits tall shrubs and overgrown hedges.
products.bestFor: Tall shrubs and high branches where reach matters.
pros: 36 inch length for reach and leverage
cons: Capacity and head type need a page check
Long handles are hard to place in dense growth

products.name: Prunrt Telescopic Lopper, 26 to 40 Inch Sync Drive
products.description:
Prunrt offers telescopic handles that extend from 26 to 40 inches and a sync drive leverage mechanism the listing says delivers up to 3 times more force. It also lists a fully hardened anvil steel blade with a low friction non stick coating and rust resistance.

The adjustable length lets you choke up for control or extend for reach, which is a flexibility fixed length loppers lack. Telescoping adds a locking joint that must be tightened properly, and a longer extension flexes more under load. The listing mentions anvil steel, so it is best suited to dry wood, though the capacity number is cut off in the text we saw, so check the product page.

In use, extend to the length you need, lock it firmly and make controlled cuts. Compared with the fixed 32 inch Fiskars it adds adjustability, and compared with the Hickok 36 inch it trades some rigidity for flexibility. It suits yards with mixed pruning heights.
products.bestFor: Mixed pruning jobs that need adjustable reach and extra force.
pros: Sync drive for up to 3 times force

products.name: FELCO F211-50 20 Inch Swiss Made Loppers
products.description:
FELCO is the compact precision option, a 20 inch lopper with lightweight aluminum handles, carbon steel blades for edge retention and a micrometric adjustment mechanism that makes blade replacement easy. It is Swiss made, according to the listing.

The short handle gives control rather than power, which suits careful shaping of ornamental shrubs and tight spaces. The listing does not state a cutting capacity or head type in the text we evaluated, so check the product page for those facts. A replaceable blade design is a long term value, because the tool can be maintained rather than thrown away.

In ownership the adjustment and serviceability are the point. Compared with the 36 inch Hickok it offers far less reach, and compared with the Fiskars PowerGear2 it has no named leverage system. It suits owners who value maintenance, control and precision cuts.
products.bestFor: Careful shaping in tight spaces and owners who value serviceability.
pros: Carbon steel blades for edge retention

buyingCriteria.explanation: Bypass blades slice past a hook like scissors and are better for live green wood, which the Fiskars PowerGear2 and Corona X Series Pro use. Anvil heads press a blade onto a flat plate and suit dry dead wood, like the TABOR GG12A, but can crush live stems. Match the head to the wood you cut most. If your yard has both, the bypass is the safer all rounder and an anvil is a specialist.

Capacity is the largest branch diameter the tool claims to cut, with Corona at 2-1/4 inches, Fiskars PowerGear2 and TABOR at 2 inches. A rough guide is up to 1 inch for light use, 1 to 1.5 inches for general work and up to 2 inches for heavy duty. The number assumes fresh green wood, so dry hardwood is harder than it suggests. If a branch does not fit comfortably in the jaws, use a pruning saw.

Handles of 18 to 22 inches give control, 24 to 30 inches balance reach and leverage, and longer handles give more leverage and reach but add weight. The FELCO is 20 inches, the TABOR is 30, the Fiskars is 32 and the Hickok is 36. Longer is harder to place precisely in dense growth. Choose by your tallest pruning job and your arm strength.

Compound, geared or ratcheting mechanisms multiply force so you can cut thicker wood with less hand strength. Fiskars PowerGear2, TABOR compound action and Prunrt sync drive each multiply leverage in different ways. A ratchet clicks to build force in steps. If hand strength is limited, a leverage mechanism matters more than a longer handle.

A lopper is held overhead and swung repeatedly, so weight adds fatigue. Hickok and FELCO use aluminum handles to stay light, while Corona is a heavy duty pro build. Check the product page for weight, because the listings here do not all state it. Lighter tools reduce fatigue but can flex under big loads.

A dull blade needs more force and can damage the plant, so sharpen it and wipe sap after use. FELCO offers micrometric adjustment for easy blade replacement, and Fiskars and TABOR add low friction coatings that reduce gumming. Keep the pivot snug and lightly oiled. A tool you can maintain stays useful for decades.

howWeEvaluated.title: Head type and capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated head types and capacities. Corona leads on capacity at 2-1/4 inches, Fiskars PowerGear2 and TABOR claim 2 inches, and Prunrt, Hickok and FELCO leave details to the product page.

howWeEvaluated.title: Leverage systems
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at named mechanisms. Fiskars PowerGear2, TABOR compound action and Prunrt sync drive each claim multiplied force, while Corona and FELCO do not name one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and handle length
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared lengths from FELCO at 20 inches up to Hickok at 36 inches and Prunrt at 26 to 40 inches telescopic. Length trades control for reach.

howWeEvaluated.title: Blade materials
howWeEvaluated.description: We read blade claims, from FELCO carbon steel to Hickok forged heat treated steel and the coated blades on Fiskars, TABOR and Prunrt.

howWeEvaluated.title: Listing completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We flagged listings that omit capacity or head type and told readers to check the product page.

howToChoose.intro: The head type is a decision about wood, not strength.

cards.label: Bypass
cards.text: A bypass blade slices past a hook like scissors, leaving a clean cut on live wood. Fiskars PowerGear2 and Corona X Series Pro are bypass tools. Pick bypass if most of your pruning is green growth you want to heal well.

cards.label: Anvil
cards.text: An anvil head presses the blade onto a flat plate, which cracks dry dead wood well but can crush live stems. TABOR GG12A and Prunrt use anvil style blades. Pick anvil if you mostly clear dead branches.

Prunrt Telescopic Lopper, 26 to 40 Inch Sync Drive

howToChoose.note: A telescopic handle like the Prunrt gives choice but adds a locking joint, so tighten it fully before every cut and check it again if the tool feels loose under load.

howToChoose.intro: Leverage is more important than raw capacity.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A named leverage mechanism, light handles and a head sized to the wood. A ratchet or compound action reduces the squeeze needed, and lighter aluminum reduces fatigue.

faq.q: Which is better, bypass or anvil loppers?
faq.a: Bypass suits live green wood because it slices cleanly, while anvil suits dry dead wood because it cracks through it. If you only buy one, bypass is the safer all rounder. Anvil is a specialist for deadwood.

faq.q: How thick a branch can a lopper cut?
faq.a: Stated capacities in this group run from 2 inches to 2-1/4 inches. Those numbers assume fresh green wood, and dry hardwood is harder than they suggest. If a branch does not fit comfortably in the jaws, use a pruning saw.

faq.q: Does a longer handle make a lopper better?
faq.a: It gives more leverage and reach but adds weight and makes placement harder. A 20 inch FELCO offers control, while a 36 inch Hickok gives reach. Pick the length for your tallest job and arm strength.

faq.q: How do I keep a lopper sharp?
faq.a: Wipe sap after use, sharpen the cutting edge when it starts crushing and keep the pivot snug. A dull blade needs more force and can damage the plant. Coated blades like Fiskars and TABOR reduce gumming.

faq.q: Can I cut live branches with an anvil lopper?
faq.a: You can, but it may crush the stem and leave a rougher wound. Use bypass for live growth when you can. Reserve anvil tools for dead wood.

faq.q: When should I use a saw instead?
faq.a: When a branch will not fit comfortably in the jaws or needs you to force the tool. A saw is safer on thick limbs. Pruning earlier keeps branches within lopper range.

faq.q: What length should I buy for a small yard with dense shrubs?
faq.a: A shorter tool gives control in tight growth, and 18 to 22 inches is the usual control range, which is where the 20 inch FELCO F211-50 sits. Medium handles of 24 to 30 inches, like the 30 inch TABOR GG12A, balance reach and leverage for most gardens. A 36 inch Hickok is harder to place between stems, so save it for tall hedges. If you cut mostly thin growth, extra length only adds weight.

faq.q: Why do my cuts look crushed or ragged?
faq.a: Usually the blade is dull, the branch is too thick for the jaws, or an anvil head is being used on live wood. Sharpen the edge, switch to a bypass tool like the Fiskars PowerGear2 for green stems, and move to a saw when the branch does not fit comfortably. Forcing a lopper through a thick limb also loosens the pivot. Check that the pivot bolt is snug before the next job.
